instantiated_cells.justification: The statute defines "lobbying" by the subject matter of influence attempts (legislation, regulations, procurements, etc.) but does not enumerate communication modalities such as oral, written, electronic, virtual, meetings, events, phone calls, or emails.

"Lobbyist" is defined broadly as "every person or organization retained, employed or designated by any client to engage in lobbying," and "organization" includes corporations, companies, foundations, associations, colleges, labor organizations, firms, partnerships, societies, joint stock companies, state agencies or public corporations; government employees acting in official duties are excluded, but public corporations are included.

The statute defines "public corporation" as a municipal corporation, district corporation, or public benefit corporation as defined in section 66 of the general construction law, which serves as the public entity definition.

The statute exempts from registration any lobbyist who does not expend, incur, or receive more than $5,000 of reportable compensation and expenses for lobbying, constituting a materiality threshold for coverage.
Lobbying expressly includes attempts to influence passage or defeat of legislation by either house of the state legislature, approval/disapproval by the governor, and gubernatorial executive orders.

Lobbying targets include the legislature, governor, state agencies (and their officers/employees), and the definition of "public official" expressly covers the governor, legislators, state department heads, officers/employees of state agencies, and municipal officers/employees.
Lobbying expressly includes attempts to influence passage or defeat of legislation by either house of the state legislature, approval/disapproval by the governor, and gubernatorial executive orders.
Lobbying expressly includes attempts to influence passage or defeat of legislation by either house of the state legislature, approval/disapproval by the governor, and gubernatorial executive orders.
Lobbying expressly includes attempts to influence passage or defeat of legislation by either house of the state legislature, approval/disapproval by the governor, and gubernatorial executive orders.

The statute targets the legislative and executive branches and defines "public official" to include the governor, legislators, heads of state departments and their deputies/assistants, officers and employees of state departments/agencies, legislative officers and employees, and municipal officers and employees.

The "lobbyist" definition expressly excludes any officer, director, trustee, employee, counsel or agent of the state or any municipality when discharging their official duties, so elected officials/public appointees are not required to register for such activities.
Public employees discharging official duties are excluded from the "lobbyist" definition without reference to compensation, expenditure, or time thresholds applicable to them as public employees.

The definitions of lobbyist, client, and organization rely on retention/employment/designation relationships and organizational form, not on whether the entity holds a public charter or special government protection.
The definitions of lobbyist and client turn on retention, employment, or designation to engage in lobbying, not on ownership criteria.

The definitions of lobbyist, client, and organization do not depend on revenue structure or composition; coverage thresholds are based on compensation/expenses for lobbying, not on the source or structure of the entity's revenue.
